entries.test: Public statements and reporting preceding November 24, 2024 would show whether a substantial retreat from earlier AI scaling claims had begun.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion gives 'retrenchment' a concrete meaning: retreat from earlier scaling predictions.

entries.test: Contemporaneous public statements and reporting would show whether acknowledgment of unreleased models falling short of scaling predictions was widespread in the AI field.
entries.note: Quiet acknowledgments can be documented through public reporting; they are not necessarily inaccessible private beliefs.

entries.test: Published training-compute scaling predictions and actual model performance available for the period would show whether longer training continued to deliver the predicted gains.
entries.note: In context, 'not holding' concerns predicted performance gains, rather than the absence of any improvement.
This is advice to exercise financial caution.

entries.test: The original and newer scaling research would establish whether the relationships are empirical fits to model experiments rather than physical laws.
entries.note: This makes a concrete claim about the scientific status and basis of the relationships.

entries.test: Public experiments extending post-training and inference-time compute would show whether the claimed scaling relationships eventually break down.
entries.note: This is a firm prediction without a deadline.

entries.test: Public GPU-use and cost measurements together with accuracy-versus-compute results across tasks would establish the added expense and inconsistent gains of inference-time scaling.
entries.note: The statement explicitly attributes expense to increased GPU time and also asserts unreliable benefits.

entries.test: OpenAI's cited o1 research post would show whether increased test-time compute improves performance on some problems but fails to improve it on others.
entries.note: Comparing o1 with GPT-4 alone would not establish the effect of increasing test-time compute.

entries.test: Public head-to-head evaluations of the contemporaneous o1 and GPT-4 models would show whether o1 ties or underperforms GPT-4 on any tested tasks.
entries.note: The claim requires some cases, not general inferiority.
'My guess' explicitly hedges the claim, and 'not so well' is weaker than 'poorly.' He describes a performance pattern without explicitly asserting its cause.

entries.test: Public evaluations across comparable tasks would show whether o1's improvements over GPT-4 were substantially less consistent than GPT-4's improvements over GPT-3.
entries.note: 'Its predecessors' broadens the contextual comparison with GPT-4 to an unspecified group of models.
The proposition drops 'if they ever were,' implying a prior status Marcus questions. 'Greatly devalued' is an evaluative judgment about terminology.

entries.test: Public formulations of the earlier and newer scaling claims and documented investment rationales would show whether the newer claims provide substantially less specific performance predictions.
entries.note: 'Amounts to trial and error' strengthens the comparative 'much more' formulation. Context grounds 'weaker' in predictive specificity.
The wet-plates analogy conveys futility without specifying a testable outcome or threshold.
He advocates fresh invention beyond scaling.
'Only take us so far' identifies neither an AI capability ceiling nor a particular scaling relationship whose failure would settle this broad claim.
